1.q: How many bytes are in 1 TB, using the course rule? Type the number.
In what unit is a processor's clock speed written? (abbreviation)

2.q: Type the command that lists the processes you own (course form, no dash).
Type the command that brings a suspended process back to the foreground.

3.q: Command to search a file for lines that match "bbt", ignoring case: ___ FILENAME
Command to show the first 8 lines of a file: ___ FILENAME
Command to extract fields 10 and 20 from a file, using a comma as the delimiter: ___ FILENAME
Command to sort lines of text numerically: ___ FILENAME
Command to list all files that have vibe in the middle, with 1 or more characters before and after it.
Type a pipeline that prints the lowest price (column 3) of FILENAME, skipping the header.
Type a pipeline that counts the unique foods (column 2) in FILENAME, skipping the header.
a: tail -n +2 FILENAME | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq | wc -l

4.q: Command to give the owner read permission only, and group and world no permissions: ___ FILENAME (format COMMAND X=Y,AB=)
Command to remove write permission from group and world on the folder shared.
Command that prints your current absolute path.
Command to list the current directory including hidden files.
Command that deletes the directory old together with everything inside it.

5.q: In the hostname node7.cluster.spider.net, the computer name is ____
In the hostname cute.labubu.flushie.biz, the Top-Level Domain is ____
What is the hostname equivalent of 127.0.0.1?
Command to resolve x.com using the nameserver 1.1.1.1, with a short answer.
Command to test whether smoo.com has a server process listening on port 443.
In a typical home network, the default nameserver runs on the home network's ____

6.q: For a web client to connect to a web server, it must know the server's IP address and ____ number.
Command to view only the HTTP response body for https://x.com (httpie).
Which HTML element inserts a line break? Type the tag.
A page references three images. How many files does the browser download in total?

8.q: Connect to the instance at 3.1.2.4 as ec2-user using the key file is114-keypair.pem.

9.q: Encrypt FUNDAMENTAL with a Caesar shift of 3.
Decrypt FRPSXWHU with a Caesar shift of 3.

10.q: Which port do the sensors use to send encrypted telemetry to the cloud?

1.q: Which statements about RAM and storage are true?
o: The CPU executes a program directly from storage.
More storage lets you run more programs at once.
When power is lost, a running process is lost but its program file remains.
1.e: Storage holds the permanent copy; RAM holds the working copy.

1.q: Which statements about a laptop specification are correct?
o: "1920 × 1080" is the resolution in pixels, width by height.
"15-inch" is the diagonal length of the display.
"12 MB cache" is fast volatile memory inside the CPU.
1.e: Each spec line names one component and its measure.

1.q: Which statements about embedded systems are true?
o: They are computers dedicated to a narrow range of functions.
They can be found in microwaves, cars and watches.
They have no processor or memory.
They are part of a larger system.
1.e: Same resources as a normal computer, in a small dedicated package.

1.q: Which statements describe what happens when you open a browser?
o: The program is loaded from storage into RAM.
RAM supplies instructions and data to the CPU.
The GPU can handle graphics such as video and animation.
The CPU copies the program back to cache permanently.
Results can be saved back to storage.
1.e: Storage → RAM → CPU → results, with the GPU handling graphics.

2.q: Which are roles of an operating system?
o: Manage resources such as memory and storage.
Provide an interface for a human to interact with the computer.
Allow application programs to use those resources.
Share resources among programs that want them.
2.e: All roles revolve around sharing resources nicely.

2.q: Which statements about programs and processes are true?
o: A program is an executable file stored in non-volatile storage.
A process is a program in execution.
When power is cut, the process terminates but the program remains.
Task Manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (macOS) shows processes.

2.q: A user presses Ctrl-Z while top is running, then types fg and presses Ctrl-C. Which statements are correct?
o: Ctrl-Z suspended top and moved it out of the foreground.
Ctrl-Z killed top and freed all its RAM.
2.e: Pause is not kill: a suspended process keeps its RAM.

2.q: Which statements about booting are correct?
o: Firmware loads the OS from non-volatile storage into memory.
The OS then takes control of the computer.
The OS must already be in RAM when power is applied.
Storage must hold the OS for it to start.
Booting happens each time power is applied.
2.e: The OS lives in storage and is loaded into memory at boot.

3.q: Which command and purpose pairs are correct?
o: head: display the end of a file
3.e: head shows the beginning, tail the end, sort sorts.

3.q: FILENAME has a header row. Which commands correctly count the unique foods?
3.e: uniq needs sorted input, or use sort -u.

3.q: Which commands give the number of lines that contain "Sushi" in FILENAME?
3.e: grep selects the lines and wc -l counts them.

3.q: Which statements about sort are correct?
3.e: Use -n whenever the column is numeric.

3.q: Which statements about redirection are correct?
o: > creates the file or overwrites it.
>> appends to the end of the file.
> file.txt on its own empties the file but keeps it.
echo "a" >> f run twice leaves two lines.
3.e: One arrow overwrites, two arrows append.

3.q: Which wildcard statements are correct?
o: ls s?m? matches four-letter names with s first and m third.
ls so* lists names starting with so.
3.e: Star is many, question mark is one.

3.q: Which statements about uniq options are correct?
o: -c prefixes each line with its count.
-d shows only lines that are duplicated.
-u shows only lines that appear once.
All of them work on adjacent lines, so sort first.

4.q: The current directory is /home/jones. Which resolutions are correct?
4.e: Apply each .. one level at a time.

4.q: Which statements about permissions on a directory are correct?
o: r lets you list its contents.
x lets you enter it with cd.
w lets you create, delete or rename items inside.
x lets you edit the files inside.
Without x, cd fails even if you can read the directory.
4.e: Directory x is about entering, not editing files.

4.q: Which commands make notes.txt readable and writable by the owner only?
o: chmod go-rwx notes.txt, if the owner already has rw
4.e: Symbolic chmod has no spaces; go- removes group and world rights.

4.q: Which statements about file types are correct?
o: Renaming virus.exe to funny-cat.jpg does not change what the file is.
Text files are not stored as binary digits.
The extension helps the OS choose a program to open the file.
A file can be converted by changing its extension.
4.e: All data is bits; the extension is only a hint.

4.q: Which statements about PATH are correct?
o: It is a list of directories searched for executables.
The OS searches them in order and runs the first match.
It lists every file on the computer.
If printall is in a PATH directory you can run it by name from any directory.
It is only used on Windows.

5.q: Which statements about packet switching are correct?
o: Routers know the full path from sender to receiver.
5.e: Independent routes, reassembly at the end.

5.q: Which of these must a data packet include?
5.e: IP gets it to the computer; the port gets it to the process.

5.q: Which statements about ping are correct?
o: A reply shows the host is reachable and gives the round-trip time.
A timeout proves the host is down.
A name-resolution failure points to a DNS problem.
ping tells you whether a port is open.
ping can show the IP address of a hostname.
5.e: No reply is inconclusive, since some hosts ignore pings.

5.q: Which statements about nmap port states are correct?
o: Closed: the host answers and no application listens on that port.
Filtered: a firewall blocks the probe, so the state is unknown.
Closed and filtered mean the same.
Filtered always means the server is down.

5.q: Which tool and purpose pairs are correct?
o: ping: checks whether a host is reachable
dig: finds the IP address of a domain
nmap: checks which ports are open on a host
5.e: Three tools, three questions: reachable? which IP? which ports?

6.q: Which statements about HTML and CSS are correct?
o: The browser honours every extra blank line you type in HTML.
Tags are written in angle brackets.
Improperly nested tags can give unpredictable rendering.
6.e: Content and look are separate concerns.

6.q: Which statements about the parts of a URL are correct?
o: The scheme says how the resource is accessed, such as http or https.
The host tells the client which server to contact.
If the port is omitted, http uses 80 and https uses 443.
The anchor starts with ? and ends with &.
The query holds key-value pairs, first after ? then separated by &.
6.e: scheme://host:port/path?query#anchor

6.q: Which statements about httpie and browsers are correct?
o: A browser shows the rendered page.
"View Source" in a browser shows the raw HTML.
6.e: Source and rendered pages differ.

6.q: A server is running on port 8000 of your own computer. Which statements are correct?
o: After Ctrl-C stops the server, nmap shows closed.
After the server stops, the browser cannot connect.
nmap shows filtered while the server runs on localhost.
A second server needs a different port, such as 9000.
6.e: Open while running, closed after stopping.

6.q: What URL(s) can clients on the same computer use to reach their own HTTP server?
6.e: localhost is the name for 127.0.0.1.

6.q: A user types https://1.2.3.4/page.html into Chrome. Which statements are correct?
o: The web server process on 1.2.3.4 is identified by its IP address and port number 443.
Chrome is the web client and runs on the user's laptop.
Chrome requests the file page.html from the server.
The server process requests page.html from Chrome.
The page is rendered on the user's laptop.
6.e: The client asks and the server answers; IP plus port locate the server process.

6.q:
Computer W (IP 1.2.3.4) will host a website on port 8888, and computer X will access it. The steps are:
Step 1: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is closed.
Step 2: On W, start the web server on port 8888.
Step 3: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 4: On X, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 5: On X, visit http://1.2.3.4:8888 and check that the page appears.
Which steps use nmap to check a port's state?
6.e: Steps 2 and 5 start the server and browse; the other three are nmap checks.

7.q: Which statements about a home LAN are correct?
o: The ONT converts optical signals from the ISP into electrical signals.
A consumer router is often a router, switch and Wi-Fi access point in one.
The router is the default gateway.
The router has only a private IP.
A home router has both a public and a private IP.
7.e: The router faces both the ISP and the LAN.
Check the boundaries of the 172 range.

7.q: Which statements about public and private IP addresses are correct?
o: A public IP is globally unique.
A private IP can be reused in different LANs.
A private IP is routable on the Internet.
ISPs obtain public IPs from regional registries such as APNIC.
A home router's public IP may change unless a static IP is bought.
7.e: Public is unique and routable; private is local.

7.q: A laptop at 192.168.0.12 requests a web page. Which statements about NAT are correct?
o: The router replaces the private source address and port with its public address and a port.
The router records the mapping in a table.
The reply goes to the laptop's private IP directly across the Internet.
The router looks up the table and sends the reply to the laptop.
Websites see the router's public IP for all devices behind it.

7.q: A phone is on mobile data and then on home Wi-Fi. Which statements are generally justified?
o: On Wi-Fi its IP is usually private.
On mobile data its IP is usually public.
Its IP is always the same in both cases.
A website sees the router's public IP for a Wi-Fi connection.
Private IPs are used on the Internet backbone.
7.e: What a website sees may differ from the device's own address.

8.q: Which statements about cloud computing are correct?
o: Resources are provided by a third party and managed over the Internet.
On-premise means the organisation owns and manages its own servers.
In the cloud you pay for the hardware whether or not you use it.
Gmail is an example of a cloud service.
Users need not care where their resources are physically located.

8.q: Which statements about cloud deployment models are correct?
o: A public cloud is open to any subscriber.
A private cloud is for one organisation.
A community cloud is shared by organisations with similar needs.
A hybrid cloud combines other models.
The model depends on where the hardware is.
8.e: It is about who can use it, not where it sits.

8.q: Which statements about ssh -i is114-keypair.pem ec2-user@IP are correct?
o: ec2-user is the login user on the instance.
IP is the public IPv4 address of the instance.
The key file should have permissions like chmod u=rw,go=.
The command works with the key readable by everyone.

8.q: A web server runs on port 80 of an EC2 instance, but nobody can browse to it and nmap says filtered. Which statements are justified?
o: The security group may lack an inbound rule for port 80.
The server may be running perfectly.
Adding an inbound rule for 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 should fix it.

8.q: Which security group settings follow typical good practice?
o: Allow 22 only from administrator IP addresses.
A security group acts as a firewall for the instance.

8.q: A company keeps sensitive financial data on private clusters and serves a public web app from AWS. Which statements are correct?
o: It uses both private and public resources.
It is an on-premise only model.

9.q: Which statements about the CIA triad are correct?
o: Confidentiality is protection from unauthorised access.
Integrity is modification only by appropriate mechanisms.
Availability is authorised access when needed.
A DoS flood is an attack on availability.

9.q: Which scenarios map correctly to a CIA pillar?
o: A web root pointing at private files: confidentiality is broken.
A tampered account balance: integrity is broken.
An unreachable server: availability is broken.
Data corrupted by a transmission error: integrity is broken.
A DoS flood: confidentiality is broken.

9.q: Which statements about authentication are correct?
o: Something you know includes a password or PIN.
Something you have includes a smart card or token.
Something you are is a biometric trait such as a fingerprint.
Two-factor authentication needs two different kinds of credential.
SMS one-time codes are the strongest factor.

9.q: Which statements about cryptography vocabulary are correct?
o: Plaintext is readable and ciphertext is not.
A cipher is the algorithm and the key guides it.
Cryptanalysis is decrypting without knowing the cipher or key.
A Caesar cipher is hard for modern computers to break.
Decrypting FRPSXWHU with shift 3 gives COMPUTER.
9.e: Substitution ciphers are weak; decryption shifts each letter back.

9.q: Which statements about symmetric and public-key cryptography are correct?
o: Symmetric schemes use the same key to encrypt and decrypt.
Symmetric schemes have a key-distribution problem.
Public-key cryptography uses a public and a private key.
The public key encrypts and the private key decrypts.
The private key is sent along with the message.
9.e: The private key is never transmitted.

10.q: Which tiers and concepts are matched correctly?
o: Tier 1: sensors and wearables, embedded systems, Bluetooth.
Tier 2: ONT and router, DHCP and NAT.
Tier 3: AWS EC2, public cloud virtualisation.
Tier 4: Python web server and ML engine.
10.e: Each tier has its own vocabulary.

10.q: Which statements about the perimeter security are correct?
o: Ports 80 and 443 are open to 0.0.0.0/0 so clients and sensors can connect.
Port 22 is restricted to administrator IPs.
The private key is protected with chmod u=rw,go=.
The private key is stored in authorized_keys.
10.e: Open what must be public; lock down the rest.

10.q: The security group lacks a rule for port 443, yet the web server runs on 443. Which statements are correct?
o: Sensors cannot deliver telemetry over HTTPS.
nmap from the Internet reports 443 as filtered.
Adding an inbound rule for 443 fixes the symptom.
Alerts to caregivers might be delayed or lost.
10.e: The server is reachable only if a rule allows it.

lessons.title: Computer Hardware
lessons.goal: Read a laptop specification and explain what the processor, RAM, storage, GPU and ports each do.
lessons.subtitle: Read a laptop specification and explain what the processor, RAM, storage, GPU and ports each do.
lessons.html:
💡 OverviewEvery later topic, from processes to the cloud, runs on these parts. Knowing which part does what lets you explain why a computer is slow or why work is lost.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Hardware vs software→2Reading a laptop specification line by line→3Metric prefixes — powers of ten→4The processor (CPU)→5Memory (RAM) vs storage — the central compar…→6How it all works together (when you open a b…→7GPU, display, ports, wireless→8Embedded systems and the micro:bit→9Hardware gotchas
⚡ At a glance — the machine
Storage (non-volatile)→RAM (volatile)→Cache→CPU cores→Display, ports
Easily confused terms
TermWhat it isNot to be confused with
RAMVolatile main memory that holds the programs and data in use now.Fast and empties at power-off; not the same as storage.
Storage (SSD/HDD)Non-volatile secondary memory for the OS, apps and files.Keeps data without power; slower than RAM.
CacheVery fast volatile memory on or near the CPU.Checked first, before RAM and storage.
CoreOne independent processor inside a multi-core CPU.More cores help parallel work and use more power.
GHzClock speed in billions of cycles per second.A speed unit, not a size unit.
🗺️ The whole course in one picture

IS114 walks bottom-up from the machine to the Internet and security: hardware → operating system → files & permissions → networks → the Web → LANs/NAT → cloud → security. Each layer relies on the one before it: a process (Chapter 2) needs RAM (Chapter 1); a web server (Chapter 6) is a process (Chapter 2) that listens on a port (Chapter 5) and serves files from a directory (Chapter 4); a cloud VM (Chapter 8) is just a remote Linux machine you reach by SSH using a protected key file (Chapters 4 and 9).

Concept map of the whole course. Read it clockwise from Chapter 1; each branch is a Part of these notes.

flowchart TD
  A[Storage SSD/HDD<br/>non-volatile] -->|program loaded into| B[RAM<br/>volatile]
  B -->|instructions and data| C[Cache]
  C --> D[CPU cores<br/>fetch decode execute]
  D --> E[GPU graphics]

  B -->|save| A
  D --> F[Display and ports]

How storage, RAM, cache and CPU cooperate when you open a program (cache position inferred from). Note the CPU never executes straight from storage — programs are copied into RAM first.

1.1Hardware vs software
TermMeaning
HardwarePhysical parts you can touch; "visible even when powered off", consuming no electricity. Examples: processor, memory, storage, battery, keyboard, screen, ports.
SoftwarePrograms and data that run on hardware (OS, web browser, word processor).

A computing system = hardware + software. In the Week 1 specification, the single software item is Windows 11 Home.

1.2Reading a laptop specification line by line

The course reference specification:

Spec lineMeaning
Intel Core i7CPU model — a high-performance processor.
2.8 GHzClock speed = 2.8 billion cycles per second.
Quad-Core4 cores for parallel processing / better multitasking.
12 MB Intel Smart CacheVery fast volatile memory inside the CPU; 12 MB = 12 million bytes.
15-inch HD LED display (1920 × 1080)15 inches = diagonal screen size; HD = High Definition; LED = Light-Emitting Diode backlight (energy-efficient, long-lasting, mercury-free); 1920 × 1080 = resolution in pixels, width × height.
Intel Iris Xe GPUGraphics Processing Unit: handles graphics (games, video, animation); relieves the CPU.
20 GB RAMRandom Access Memory (main memory); 20 GB = 20 billion bytes; volatile.
1 TB SSDSolid-State Drive (secondary storage); 1 TB = 1 trillion bytes; non-volatile; faster and more durable than HDD (no moving parts).
WiFi 7, Bluetooth 5WiFi: wireless internet (long range). Bluetooth: short-range wireless for keyboards, earphones, phone syncing.
2 USB Type-C portsUniversal Serial Bus: connects external devices (flash drives, monitors, phones).
1 HDMI portHigh-Definition Multimedia Interface: sends video and audio to TVs/projectors.
3 kgWeight.
Windows 11 HomePre-installed operating system (software).
1.3Metric prefixes — powers of ten
PrefixSymbolValueIn bytes
Kilo-K10³1,000 B
Mega-M10⁶1,000,000 B
Giga-G10⁹1,000,000,000 B
Tera-T10¹²1,000,000,000,000 B
Peta-P10¹⁵1 quadrillion B

(in words: kilo = thousand, mega = million, giga = billion, tera = trillion, peta = quadrillion)

Course rule: use powers of 10 (1 KB = 1,000 B). Ignore binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB). shows the prefixes up to Tera; Peta appears in and.

Worked example. The spec lists 20 GB RAM. 20 GB = 20 × 10⁹ = 20,000,000,000 bytes. If one ASCII character is 1 byte, RAM could in principle hold 20 billion characters (ignoring OS overhead). Emoji are usually 4 bytes each, so the same RAM holds roughly 5×10⁹ emoji.

1.4The processor (CPU)

Synonyms: CPU, Central Processing Unit, microprocessor, microcontroller. Think of it as "the brain".

PartWhat it isWhy it matters
FunctionFetch instructions and data from memory, decode, execute; process data (text, images, numbers)The only component that actually computes.
ClockA centrally generated series of electrical pulses that coordinates all actions in the computer. Measured in Hz (cycles per second); 2.8 GHz = 2.8 billion cycles/second.The "conductor's baton" . Higher GHz → more cycles per second.
CoresA multi-core CPU has several independent processors in one chip (Dual/Quad/Hexa).More cores = better performance and higher power usage (and more heat and cost).
CacheVery fast volatile memory on/near the CPU storing frequently used data/instructions (typically 8–12 MB).Avoids waiting on slower RAM.

Lookup order when the CPU needs data: cache (fastest) → RAM → storage (slowest, last resort). The CPU tries the fastest place first to avoid delays. Note states this "is not stated explicitly in the notes, and requires inference".

1.5Memory (RAM) vs storage — the central comparison
AttributeMemory (RAM)Storage (SSD/HDD)
SynonymsRAM, primary storage/memory, main memory, volatile memorySecondary storage, disk, non-volatile memory
VolatilityVolatile — all contents lost when power is offNon-volatile — retained without power
RoleHolds the OS, programs and data currently in useLong-term storage of OS, apps, files
CPU accessCPU reads from and writes to it directly; programs execute from hereCPU cannot execute from storage; program must be loaded into RAM first
Typical capacity4–32 GB in laptops/phones;: 4 GB basic, 16 GB standard, 32 GB high-end200 GB–1 TB;: 256 GB–1 TB laptops, several TB desktops/servers; summary table 256 GB–2 TB
SpeedFast (but slower than cache)Slower ("storage is slower than RAM but permanent")
Effect of too littleOS closes programs to free space; too many apps feel sluggishLess room for files and apps

Storage types: SSD — no moving parts, fast, durable, expensive; HDD — spinning disk, slower, cheaper, more fragile; SD card — removable (cameras, phones).

Hardware summary table:

ComponentCategoryVolatile?SpeedTypical sizeRole
CPUProcessorn/aFastestn/aExecutes instructions
CacheMemoryYesVery fast8–12 MBSpeeds up CPU access
RAMMemoryYesFast4–32 GBRun programs & store active data
SSD/HDDStorageNoSlower256 GB–2 TBStore OS, apps, files long-term
GPUProcessorn/aFastIntegrated or dedicatedHandle graphics

Unsaved work. Because RAM is volatile, anything you are editing that hasn't been saved to storage is lost immediately on sudden power loss. A running process dies on power-off, while its program file survives on storage (see §2.5).

  • Why a fast CPU can still be slow: if storage is slow, data loads slowly and the CPU sits idle waiting for it — storage becomes the bottleneck, not the processor.
  • Why the CPU does not just use storage: RAM is the fast working area; the number of programs that can run at once is limited by RAM, not by disk size.
🧩 Pause & recall — Why must a program be copied into RAM before it runs?
Answer: The CPU reads and executes instructions from RAM, not directly from storage. Storage is the permanent copy; RAM is the working copy.
1.6How it all works together (when you open a browser)
  1. Storage loads the program into RAM.
  2. RAM supplies data/instructions to the CPU.
  3. CPU executes instructions and processes data.
  4. GPU handles graphics (video, animations).
  5. Results are shown on screen and saved back to storage if needed.

"This cycle runs millions of times per second." The von Neumann architecture: instructions (software) and data are both stored in the memory unit.

1.7GPU, display, ports, wireless
  • GPU: a separate processor for graphics; frees the CPU; also used for machine-learning tasks and parallel matrix computations.
  • Display: size = diagonal of the screen; resolution = pixels wide × high (1920 × 1080 → 1,920 pixels across, 1,080 down).
  • USB: standardised bidirectional interface for data and power. HDMI: uncompressed digital audio + video to monitors/TVs.
  • Bluetooth: short range, low power → ideal for keyboards, mice, earphones.
  • Why a GPU matters for gaming: rendering fast, complex images every frame would overwhelm the main processor, so the GPU takes that job.
1.8Embedded systems and the micro:bit

An embedded system is a computer dedicated to a narrow range of functions as part of a larger system — found in microwaves, cars, watches, medical equipment, smart appliances.

The BBC micro:bit v2 is a tiny embedded computer with a processor, memory, storage and sensors; in the lab it is "a platform to practice coding and sensor integration". It demonstrates that the same three resources (processor, memory, storage) exist even in a tiny device.

1.9Hardware gotchas
  • Memory ≠ storage. A big disk does not let you run more programs at once; RAM does. (A machine with lots of storage but little RAM still feels slow when many apps run.)
  • Storage is not "executed" directly. The CPU runs programs from RAM.
  • Prefix confusion: 1 TB = 10¹² bytes in this course, not 2⁴⁰.
  • Quad-Core ≠ 4× faster in every case; it helps parallel work, and costs power.
  • 15-inch is the diagonal, not width.
Chapter summary
  • CPU = fetch, decode, execute; clock speed is in GHz; more cores help parallel work.
  • Lookup order for data: cache, then RAM, then storage.
  • RAM is volatile and holds what is running; storage is non-volatile and holds what is saved.
  • Programs are copied from storage into RAM before the CPU runs them.
  • 1 KB = 1,000 B, 1 MB = 10⁶ B, 1 GB = 10⁹ B, 1 TB = 10¹² B.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Hardwaretap to flip
The physical parts of a computer that you can touch, such as the processor, memory, storage and ports.
Softwaretap to flip
Programs and data that run on the hardware, including the operating system and applications.
CPU (processor)tap to flip
Fetches, decodes and executes instructions and processes data; the only part that actually computes.
Clock speed (GHz)tap to flip
Cycles per second. 2.8 GHz is 2.8 billion cycles per second.
Coretap to flip
An independent processor inside a multi-core CPU. More cores help parallel work but cost more power.
Cachetap to flip
Very fast volatile memory on or near the CPU that holds frequently used data. Checked before RAM.
➡ Where next? Hardware does nothing alone. Next, the operating system decides which program gets the CPU, RAM and storage.

1Software categories→2Roles of an OS — "sharing nicely"→3Why Linux?→4GUI vs CLI→5Program vs process→6Process control commands

TermWhat it isNot to be confused with
Application softwarePrograms written to solve a user need.Firefox, Office, games.
System softwareSoftware that manages the computer at a basic level.Windows, Linux, macOS.
ProgramAn executable file stored on disk.Sits in storage and survives power-off.
ProcessA program in execution.Lives in RAM and ends at power-off.
Foreground / backgroundForeground is what you interact with; background runs without interaction.Ctrl-z suspends; bg and fg resume.
2.1Software categories
CategoryDefinitionExamples
Application softwareWritten to address specific needs / solve real-world problemsTerminal, Microsoft Office, Firefox, Chrome, games, social media, AI tools
System softwareManages a computer system at a fundamental level; provides tools for creating and running application software, often interacts directly with hardwareWindows, Linux, macOS

The operating system (OS) is the core component of system software.

2.2Roles of an OS — "sharing nicely"

An OS:

  1. Manages computer resources such as memory and storage (and processors).
  2. Provides an interface through which a human can interact with the computer.
  3. Allows application programs to interact with those resources.

All roles revolve around "sharing nicely": resources are shared among programs that want them. The course notes break this into four duties:

DutyWhat it means
Processor schedulingPrograms take turns on the CPU so all make progress ()
Memory allocationIsolated RAM space per process; reclaimed on termination
Storage & I/O coordinationTurns file requests into low-level block reads/writes
User interfacesGUI and CLI

Booting: when the machine powers up, firmware loads the OS (kernel) from non-volatile storage into memory and hands control of the computer to it.

flowchart TD
  U[User] --> UI[User interface: GUI or CLI]
  UI --> OS[Operating system]
  APP[Application programs] --> OS
  OS --> CPU[Processor scheduling]
  OS --> MEM[Memory allocation]
  OS --> STO[Storage and I/O]
  CPU --> HW[Hardware]
  MEM --> HW
  STO --> HW

Caption: the OS sits between users/applications and hardware (figure re-expressed; box labels inferred). Notice every request, whether from a person or a program, passes through the OS.

2.3Why Linux?
  • Used in this course to prepare for advanced IS courses.
  • Powers over 60% of servers worldwide and all of the Top 500 supercomputers.
  • Android is built on the open-source Linux kernel.
2.4GUI vs CLI
GUICLI
InteractionClick or tap graphical elementsType commands
StrengthIntuitive for single itemsBatch processing, automation (scripting), remote administration with little bandwidth
Other names—terminal, shell, command line

Why beginners struggle with the Linux CLI: it is case-sensitive and needs precise syntax; also forgetting to check the prompt host, not using tab-completion, and confusing signals.

CLI conventions: commands are almost always lowercase; options typically come before arguments; the order of options does not matter. Tricks: Tab completion; history with ↑ / ↓; Ctrl+c stops a running command.

Which computer am I on? Look at the prompt: it shows the username and the hostname of the machine you're commanding.

  • CLI vs GUI trade-off: the CLI gives precise, quick changes and can be automated, so it wins for large-scale or repeated work; the GUI is more intuitive but slower for bulk changes. Beginner habits that avoid mistakes: re-read the syntax before pressing Enter and remember that names and options are case-sensitive.
2.5Program vs process
ProgramProcess
DefinitionAn executable file with a set of instructions (and data)A program in execution
Lives inStorage (non-volatile) — e.g. /bin/cat, C:\Windows\notepad.exeMain memory (RAM)
When power is cutRemains intactTerminates instantly (RAM is volatile)

Synonyms for program: app, application, executable file.

See them: Programs — Windows Start ➜ Settings ➜ Apps; macOS Finder ➜ Applications. Processes — Windows Task Manager; macOS Activity Monitor. Try opening and closing Notepad/Calculator and watch the process appear and vanish.

Foreground vs background: the foreground process is the one you're interacting with right now; background processes run without direct user interaction. GUI analogies: foreground ≈ maximised app you are using; background ≈ minimised/behind other windows; Ctrl-C ≈ closing the app.

  • Analogy: a program is a recipe book; a process is actually cooking from it. You can have one recipe book and several pots on the stove (one program, several processes).
  • Suspended processes are not free: a process paused with Ctrl-z is stopped but still sits in memory, so it keeps using RAM until you resume or kill it.
2.6Process control commands
CommandPurpose
ps uList processes you own (note: no dash — ps -u is ❌ in this course)
topInteractive demo process (used to practise control)
Ctrl-cTerminate (kill) the foreground process
Ctrl-zSuspend (pause) the foreground process
bgResume the most recently suspended process in the background
fgResume the most recently suspended process in the foreground

Focus on the COMMAND column of ps u — it shows the program, options and arguments.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Foreground: start command
  Foreground --> Suspended: Ctrl-z
  Suspended --> Foreground: fg
  Suspended --> Background: bg
  Background --> Foreground: fg
  Foreground --> [*]: Ctrl-c (killed)
  Background --> [*]: finishes or killed

Caption: process state control in Linux (the Background → Foreground and finish edges are inferred). A killed process frees both CPU and RAM; a suspended process uses zero CPU but still holds its RAM until resumed or killed.

Worked trace — "I pressed Ctrl-Z by mistake":

  1. You meant to kill top, but pressed Ctrl-Z. top is paused and moved out of the foreground.
  2. Type fg → it returns to the foreground.
  3. Press Ctrl-c → it is terminated.

Common beginner mistake: pressing Ctrl-Z by accident and wondering where the process went — it's paused, not gone. "Suspending vs sleeping" are different concepts, out of scope.

🧩 Pause & recall — You press Ctrl-z by mistake while running top. Is it gone?
Answer: No. It is suspended, not killed. Type fg to bring it back, then Ctrl-c to terminate it.
Chapter summary
  • The OS manages resources, provides a user interface and lets applications use resources.
  • Four duties: scheduling the CPU, allocating memory, coordinating storage and I/O, and user interfaces.
  • A program is an executable file in storage; a process is a program in execution in RAM.
  • Ctrl-c kills, Ctrl-z suspends, bg resumes in the background, fg resumes in the foreground.
  • Use ps u (no dash) to list your processes.

lessons.html:
💡 OverviewReal data arrives as text files. A short pipeline answers questions in seconds that would take minutes in a spreadsheet.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1File-system listing and file commands→2Extract, search, sort, count→3Lab 1 dataset — yum.csv→4Lab 1 — all 28 tasks with answers→5Pipeline explanations→6Redirection traces
⚡ At a glance — a counting pipeline
tail -n +2→cut -d, -f2→sort→uniq -c→sort -n -r→head
Easily confused terms
TermWhat it isNot to be confused with
cut -d -fExtracts fields (columns); -d sets the delimiter, -f the field numbers.Takes columns; grep takes rows.
grepPrints the lines that match a pattern; -i ignores case, -v inverts.Case-sensitive by default.
sortSorts lines alphabetically; -n numeric, -r reverse.Without -n, 10 sorts before 9.
uniqCollapses adjacent duplicate lines; -c counts, -d only duplicates, -u only singles.Needs sorted input.
wc -lCounts lines.Counts lines, not occurrences inside a line.
3.1File-system listing and file commands
CommandPurpose
lsList directory contents
ls -lLong format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -aInclude hidden files (names starting with .)
touch fileCreate an empty file
touch "name with spaces"Use quotes for spaces — do not use backslash \ in quizzes
cat fileDisplay the entire file
nano fileEdit a file — save Ctrl-O, exit Ctrl-X

tail file / tail -n N fileLast 10 lines / last N lines
3.2Extract, search, sort, count
CommandPurposeOptions
cutExtract fields (columns)-d delimiter, -f fields
grep "text" filePrint lines matching-i ignore case, -v invert (lines not matching)
sortSort lines (default ASCII/alphabetical)-r reverse, -n numeric
uniqRemove adjacent duplicate lines-d only duplicated lines, -u only unique lines, -c count occurrences
wcCount-l lines, -w words (-c characters appears on but says out of scope)
|Pipe: output of one command → input of the next
* ?Wildcards: * = any characters (zero or more); ? = exactly one character

Wildcard examples: ls *.csv, ls so*, ls s?m?.

Which commands accept multiple files?

Accepts several filesDoes not
cat *.csv, ls f1 f2, wc *.log, head f1 f2, tail f1 f2, sort f1 f2, grep "error" *.logcut → use cat files | cut …; uniq → use cat files | sort | uniq

Pipes: cat file | grep "dog" | sort | uniq -c; cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -c.

Redirection: > creates/overwrites; >> appends. Overwrite also truncates: > file.txt empties a file but keeps it.

flowchart LR
  A[yum.csv] -->|tail -n +2| B[no header]
  B -->|cut -d, -f2| C[food column]
  C -->|sort| D[sorted]
  D -->|uniq -c| E[count per food]
  E -->|sort -n -r| F[ranked]
  F -->|head -n 2| G[top 2]

Caption: the "top 2 most common foods" pipeline (Lab 1 task 27). Read left to right: each box is the data after the command on the arrow. sort must come before uniq because uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates.

🧩 Pause & recall — Why does sort come before uniq in a pipeline?
Answer: uniq only removes adjacent duplicates. sort puts equal lines next to each other first.
3.3Lab 1 dataset — yum.csv

Structure: 4 columns (date,food,price,rating), comma-delimited, a header row starting with #, 20 data rows. Foods that repeat: Nasi Lemak ×2, Green Milk Tea ×2, Sushi ×3.

3.4Lab 1 — all 28 tasks with answers

15Last 3 linestail -n 3 yum.csv

17Last linetail -n 1 yum.csv

19"price" column (3rd)tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f3
20Lines with "Sushi" (case-sensitive)grep "Sushi" yum.csv
21Count "Nasi Lemak"grep "Nasi Lemak" yum.csv | wc -l
22"green" regardless of casegrep -i "green" yum.csv
23Lines not containing "Chicken"grep -v "Chicken" yum.csv
24Contents without headertail -n +2 yum.csv
25Dates appearing more than oncetail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f1 | sort | uniq -d
26Foods appearing exactly oncetail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -u
27Top 2 most-common foodstail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n -r | head -n 2
28Foods costing exactly 5, sorted A→Ztail -n +2 yum.csv | grep ",5," | cut -d',' -f2 | sort

(Within a Markdown table the pipe is escaped as \|; type a plain | in the terminal.)

Worked trace — task 27 (input → output at each stage, added context computed from the dataset):

  1. tail -n +2 yum.csv → 20 data rows (header dropped; +2 means "start from line 2").
  2. cut -d',' -f2 → 20 food names.
  3. sort → alphabetical, so identical names are adjacent (Green Milk Tea, Green Milk Tea, … Sushi, Sushi, Sushi).
  4. uniq -c → counts, e.g. 3 Sushi, 2 Nasi Lemak, 2 Green Milk Tea, others 1.
  5. sort -n -r → numeric descending: 3 Sushi first, then the 2s.
  6. head -n 2 → top 2 lines. (Ties at count 2 are ordered by the secondary text of the line, so which 2 appears second is decided by the sort's tie-break — added context.)

Worked trace — task 3 vs 21: grep "Sushi" yum.csv | wc -l counts lines containing "Sushi" = 3 (2020-01-11, two on 2020-01-19). It counts lines, not occurrences within a line.

Why grep ",5," in task 28? It matches the price column exactly (,5,) and avoids prices like 15 or 50.

Best practices: always skip the header with tail -n +2 yum.csv (more reliable than grep -v "#"); use ',' as the cut delimiter for CSV; sort -n -r for descending top-N; uniq -c only after sort; chain with pipes.

Key rules recap: ps u, not ps -u · quotes for spaces, not \ · grep is case-sensitive by default · *always sort before uniq** · uniq only works on adjacent lines · cut -d',' for CSV · `= any chars,?= one char · don't usewc -c`.

3.5Pipeline explanations
  • cat yum.csv | grep "Sushi" | wc -l — stream file, keep lines containing "Sushi", count them.
  • cat yum.csv | grep -v "#date" | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c — drop the header row, extract column 2 (food), sort, count each unique food.
3.6Redirection traces
powershell
echo "monday" > file1 # file1 = monday echo "tuesday" >> file1 # appended: monday / tuesday cat file1 | wc -l # 2
powershell
echo "monday" > file1 echo "tuesday" > file1 # overwrites -> only tuesday cat file1 | wc -l # 1
Chapter summary
  • cut takes columns (-d delimiter, -f field); grep takes rows; sort orders lines; uniq collapses neighbours; wc -l counts lines.
  • Always sort before uniq, and use sort -n for numbers.
  • tail -n +2 skips a header row.
  • Pipe (|) feeds one command into the next; > overwrites and >> appends.
  • * matches any characters, ? matches exactly one.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
ls, ls -l, ls -atap to flip
List files; long format with permissions and size; include hidden files that start with a dot.
cat / head / tailtap to flip
Show the whole file, the first 10 lines, or the last 10 lines. -n N changes the count.
cuttap to flip
Extracts fields. -d sets the delimiter and -f picks fields, e.g. cut -d"," -f2.
greptap to flip
Prints lines matching a pattern. -i ignores case; -v prints lines that do not match.
sorttap to flip
Sorts lines. -r reverses; -n sorts numerically; the default is alphabetical.
uniqtap to flip
Removes adjacent duplicate lines. -c counts, -d shows duplicates, -u shows unique lines. Sort first.

lessons.html:
💡 OverviewEvery command works on files. Reading paths correctly and setting permissions is how you avoid deleting the wrong thing or exposing a private key.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
1Core definitions→2Text files vs binary files→3File types and extensions→4File operations→5Directory trees and paths→6The PATH environment variable→7Navigation and manipulation commands→8File protection and permissions→9Lab 2 — walking the is114-nav tree (27 steps)→10Filesystem gotchas
⚡ At a glance — read a path, then a permission
Root /→Directory tree→Absolute or relative→chmod u=rw,go=
Easily confused terms
TermWhat it isNot to be confused with
Absolute pathA path from the root; always starts with /.Starts with /, unique anywhere.
Relative pathA path from the current working directory.Never starts with /.
CWD (pwd)The directory you are in now.pwd prints it.
. and ... is the current directory; .. is the parent.cd . stays; cd .. goes up.
r / w / xRead, write, execute.On a directory, x means enter (cd).
4.1Core definitions
TermDefinition
FileA named collection of related data, used for organizing secondary memory; from the user's view, the smallest amount of data that can be written to storage
File systemThe operating system's logical view of the files it manages
DirectoryA named group of files (also "folder")

Why directories? They group and organise files logically, and a directory tree lets filenames be reused in different subdirectories.

Linux filenames are case-sensitive: data.txt and Data.txt are different files and can coexist. Mistyping a name can therefore act on the wrong file.

  • Why directories exist: they group files logically so that thousands of files stay findable and manageable.
4.2Text files vs binary files
Text fileBinary file
ContentCharacters from a character set (ASCII, Unicode)Data in a specific format needing special interpretation of its bits (formatting, pixels, audio…)
Human-readable?Yes — open in a text editorNo — gibberish without proper software
Examples.txt .csv .java .html .sh.docx .jpg .mp3 .pdf .exe
Editable with nano?YesNo (or you corrupt it)

Misconception alert: "Text files aren't binary" is false. Everything on a computer is stored as binary digits; "text" vs "binary" is about how the bits are interpreted — text files are chunks of 8 or 16 bits interpreted as characters. The terms "are somewhat misleading".

A .docx is binary because it embeds formatting, fonts, margins, colours and media beside the text.

  • Why binary files are less friendly: a person cannot read them directly — they need specific software to open or edit them, whereas a text file can be read in any editor.
4.3File types and extensions
  • File type = the kind of information in a file. Extension = the part after the dot (.jpg, .csv) that indicates the type; names are Filename.Extension.
  • Purpose: helps the OS choose which program opens the file (MyProg.java → code editor; family.jpg → image viewer).
  • Extension ≠ truth. Renaming virus.exe to funny-cat.jpg does not change what it is. Changing an extension (or any part of the name) does not change the contents; you can't "convert" a file by renaming.
  • What happens on double-click: OS checks extension → opens associated program → program reads the real format → mismatch gives an error.
  • Renaming an extension does not convert a file: the extension is only a label. The bytes inside keep their original format, so a program expecting the new format fails to open it.
4.4File operations
OperationCommand / meaning
Createtouch (file), mkdir (folder)
Deleterm (file); rmdir (empty dir); rm -r (dir + contents)
Open / CloseLoad into a program (e.g. nano file.txt) / exit program
Rename / Movemv old new
Copycp source dest
Readcat, head, grep
Write>, nano
Append>>
Truncate> file.txt (delete content, keep file)

TermDefinition

SubdirectoryThe directory being contained
Directory treeLogical view of nested directories
Root directoryHighest level: / (Linux), C:\ (Windows)
Current working directory (CWD)Where you are now (pwd)

Caption: a UNIX-style tree using examples /home/smith/reports/week1.txt and the two util.zip files (tree shape inferred from the paths). The two util.zip files coexist because their full paths differ.

Absolute path — begins at the root, always starts with /, unique and unambiguous. Examples: /, /bin/tar, /etc/sysconfig/clock, /home/smith/reports/week1.txt. Windows: C:\Program Files\MS Office\WinWord.exe.

Relative path — starts from the CWD, never starts with /. If CWD is /home/jones:

Relative pathResolves to

Special names: . = current directory; .. = parent directory. Find your absolute path with pwd.

4.6The PATH environment variable

PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched for executables: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/bin:/home/jones/utilities. The OS searches them in order and runs the first match. If printall is in a listed directory you can type printall from anywhere; otherwise type /home/jones/utilities/printall. Temporary addition: export PATH=$PATH:/home/jones/utilities (how to add is out of scope).

4.7Navigation and manipulation commands
CommandDescription
tree / tree FOLDERVisual tree from the current / specified folder
pwdPrint current working directory
cd / cd ~Go to home directory (same)
cd ..Up to parent
cd .Stay (no change)
cd -Previous working directory (toggle)
ls, ls -l, ls -aList; detailed; include hidden
mkdir DIR / rmdir DIRCreate / remove empty directory
rm FILE / rm -r DIRDelete file / directory recursively
mv OLD NEWMove or rename
cp F1 F2 / cp -r D1 D2Copy file / directory recursively
cat FILEDisplay
> FILE / >> FILEOverwrite / append

rm, mv, cp, > and >> "can permanently change or delete data. Use them carefully!" Deleting a directory deletes everything inside.

Hidden files: names starting with .. After mkdir one .two three, plain ls shows only one and three; use ls -a to see .two.

4.8File protection and permissions

File protection limits file access; in multi-user systems it is of primary importance. Three user categories and three permission bits:

CategorySymbolMeaning
OwneruThe user who owns the file (usually creator)
GroupgA set of users, e.g. project team
World/OtheroEveryone else with an account
(All)aall three
PermissionOn a fileOn a directory
r readView contents (cat, nano)List contents (ls)
w writeModify/overwrite/append/truncateCreate, delete, rename items inside
x executeRun as a program/scriptEnter / traverse (cd)

chmod

Syntax: chmod [who][operator][permissions] FILE, with who ∈ {u,g,o,a}, operator ∈ {+ add, - remove, = set exactly}, permissions ∈ {r,w,x}.

CommandEffect
chmod u+x script.shOwner can execute
chmod +x fileAll can execute (a+x)
chmod -x fileRemove execute from everyone
chmod go-w notes.txtRemove write from group and world
chmod u=rw,go=r fileOwner read/write; group/world read only
chmod u=rw,go= fileOnly owner read/write; nothing for group/world — private file (e.g. SSH key)
chmod u=rwx,go=rx dir/Owner full; others can enter and list but not create/delete
chmod u=r,go= FILEOwner read only, no write/execute; nothing for group/world

Note: chmod u=rw, go=r file in contains a stray space — the real syntax has no spaces around the comma.

Why must executable permission be granted explicitly? So you don't accidentally run a malicious downloaded file. A downloaded script run as ./this-is-running.sh gives Permission denied until chmod u+x this-is-running.sh.

Diagnosing permission symptoms (applications):

SymptomMissing permission
Can ls a folder ABC but cd ABC → Permission deniedx on the directory
Teammate can ls report.docx but cannot open itr on the file for their category — Group if in the file's group, otherwise World
Make a folder non-writable by everyone but the ownerchmod go-w FOLDER_NAME
World-readable, not writable fileAny user can view; cannot modify/delete
chmod u=rw,go= resultOnly owner can read/write
  • Why protection matters on shared computers: it stops other users from reading or changing your files. Giving world read and write access to sensitive files risks anyone modifying or deleting them, and data leaks or loss.
🧩 Pause & recall — You can ls a folder but cd into it says Permission denied. What is missing?
Answer: The execute (x) permission on the directory. r lets you list names; x lets you enter.

(In the source docx some of these commands are line-wrapped by the converter, e.g. cd . ./../alpha/mango; the intended commands are as shown, derived by hand-tracing the relative paths — inferred from the tree.)

Step 27 correction. The source shows ../mango/: as "(empty)". Because step 13 was cp (copy) not mv, mango still contains fomo.txt and savage.txt. Correct output: ../mango/: fomo.txt savage.txt; ../../bravo/banana/: lit.txt; ../../charlie/: grape kiwi.

flowchart LR
  A["alpha/mango<br/>fomo.txt savage.txt"] -- "cp * (copy)" --> B["bravo/banana<br/>lit.txt gucci.txt + copies"]
  C["charlie/grape<br/>vibe"] -- "mv vibe (move)" --> D["charlie/kiwi<br/>vibe added"]

Caption: cp leaves the source intact; mv removes it from the source. This is the reason step 27 must list mango as non-empty.

Concepts practised: cd navigation (steps 1,3,5,7,12,17,23,26); relative paths (all); ls (4,6,9,11,14,18,19,21,22,24,27); mkdir/rmdir (8,10); cp with * (13); rm *cc* (25); mv (20); multi-folder ls (27).

Pro tips: use tree to verify; ls before and after each operation; rmdir only works on empty folders; rm *cc* removes any name containing cc; cd .. moves up; one ls can list several folders.

4.10Filesystem gotchas
  • Case sensitivity (Data.txt ≠ data.txt).
  • Directory x is what lets you cd; r alone lists names only.
  • rmdir fails on non-empty directories; use rm -r (dangerous).
  • cp copies, mv moves. Don't assume the source disappears after cp.
  • A file that vanishes after reboot may be stored in RAM — a challenge inference: files in storage persist; RAM contents don't; the course never says files can be in RAM, but only that explains the behaviour.
  • . vs ..: cd . stays, cd .. goes up.
  • diff path1/data.csv path2/data.csv compares two files — out of scope.
  • No such file or directory after cd projects/old: first check that the path exists and that the spelling and case match exactly (Linux is case-sensitive), and that you start from the CWD you think you are in.
  • Files vanish after a reboot: suspect that the folder lives in RAM (a memory-backed area). Files on storage survive a reboot; anything in RAM is lost when power is cut.
🧪 Worked examples
Work through these by hand before you read the answer.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4.1

Copy versus move in the is114-nav lab

The setting

You are in alpha/mango, which holds fomo.txt and savage.txt. You run cp * ../../bravo/banana/. Later, in charlie/grape, you run mv vibe ../kiwi/.

What happened

After cp, both files are in banana and still in mango. After mv, vibe is in kiwi and gone from grape.

The lesson

cp leaves the source in place; mv takes it away. That is why a later ls of mango is not empty.

WORKED EXAMPLE 4.2

A downloaded script says Permission denied

The setting

You download this-is-running.sh and run ./this-is-running.sh.

What happened

The shell answers Permission denied. After chmod u+x this-is-running.sh the script runs.

The lesson

Execute permission must be granted explicitly, so a downloaded file cannot run by accident.

Chapter summary
  • A file is a named collection of data; a directory groups files; the directory tree lets names repeat in different places.
  • Absolute paths start with /; relative paths do not; . is here and .. is the parent.
  • cp copies and leaves the source; mv moves or renames; rmdir removes only empty directories; rm -r removes everything inside.
  • On a file, r reads, w modifies, x runs. On a directory, r lists, w creates and deletes, x enters.
  • chmod uses no spaces: u=rw,go=r. Extensions do not change what a file really is.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Filetap to flip
A named collection of related data used to organise secondary memory.
Directorytap to flip
A named group of files, also called a folder. A directory tree lets the same filename appear in different directories.
Text file vs binary filetap to flip
Both are stored as bits. A text file holds characters you can read in a text editor; a binary file needs special software to interpret its bits.
File extensiontap to flip
The part after the dot that suggests the file type. Renaming does not change the content or convert the file.
Absolute pathtap to flip
A path from the root directory. It always starts with / and identifies one file uniquely.
Relative pathtap to flip
A path from the current working directory. It never starts with /.
