1.q: Which component loses its contents when the power is switched off?
1.e: RAM is volatile, so unsaved work in it is lost at power-off.

1.q: A spec lists a "2.8 GHz Quad-Core" processor. What does "Quad-Core" mean?
o: The clock runs four times faster
It has four levels of cache
It can address four GB of RAM
1.e: A core is an independent processor; quad means four of them in one chip.

1.q: How many bytes is 20 GB, using the course rule?
1.e: Giga is 10⁹, so 20 GB is 20 × 10⁹ bytes.

1.q: When the CPU needs data, in which order does it look?
1.e: The CPU tries the fastest place first to avoid delays.

1.q: What role does a GPU play in a computer?
o: It permanently stores the operating system
It connects the computer to the Internet
It holds running programs while they execute
It handles graphics so the main processor is free for other tasks
1.e: GPUs also speed up machine learning.

1.q: A computer has lots of storage but little RAM. Why does it feel slow with many apps open?
o: Storage is volatile and loses its contents
The GPU runs out of pixels
RAM limits how many programs run at once; storage space does not

1.q: A fast CPU is paired with slow storage. Why can it still perform poorly?
o: The CPU waits while data loads from the slow storage

1.q: Why does a laptop need both memory and storage instead of just storage?
o: Storage is faster than memory, so memory is only a backup
Memory is fast and temporary for running programs; storage keeps data when the power is off
Memory is permanent; storage is temporary
They are two names for the same component

2.q: Which of these is system software?
2.e: System software manages the computer; Windows, Linux and macOS are examples.

2.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a process from a program?
o: A process is stored permanently on disk
A program can only run once
A process and a program are the same thing
A process is a program in execution
2.e: A program is the file; a process is the running instance in RAM.

2.q: Which key combination kills the foreground process in the Linux terminal?
Compared with a killed process, a suspended process ...
o: uses CPU time but no memory
still holds memory but uses no CPU time
2.e: Suspended = paused in memory; killed = gone.

2.q: Which resource mainly limits how many processes can run at once?
In the Linux terminal, how do you tell which computer you are working on?
o: Read the prompt, which shows the hostname
2.e: The prompt shows the hostname of the machine you control.

2.q: Which is a reason the CLI is valued over the GUI for administration?
o: It supports batch processing and automation
2.e: Commands can be scripted, repeated and used remotely.

2.q: The user clicks the Chrome icon. A Chrome ___ is started and resides in the laptop's ___.
2.e: A running program is a process, held in memory. Chrome's program file stays in storage.

2.q: Which analogy best describes a program versus a process?
o: A program is cooking; a process is the recipe book
A program is a recipe book; a process is cooking using the recipe
A program is the kitchen; a process is the ingredients
2.e: Instructions on file versus the activity of carrying them out.

3.q: Which command extracts the second comma-separated column?
3.e: cut with -d for the delimiter and -f for the field number.

3.q: Why must sort come before uniq?
3.e: Sorting puts equal lines next to each other.

3.q: What does grep -v "Chicken" file print?
o: Lines that do not contain Chicken
The number of lines with Chicken

3.q: What does rm cd ../apple/file.txt do?
o: Removes file.txt in the apple folder only
Removes a file named cd in the current folder and file.txt in the apple folder
3.e: rm treats every word after it as a file to delete.

3.q: After echo "monday" > file1 then echo "tuesday" >> file1, what does cat file1 | wc -l print?
Which pattern matches exactly one character in a filename?
3.e: ? is one character; * is any number of characters.

3.q: What does this do? cat FILENAME | grep -v "#date,food,price,rating" | cut -d, -f 2 | sort | uniq -c
o: Counts the unique foods and prints one number
For each food, shows how many times it appears
Lists the foods in reverse order
Shows only foods that appear once
3.e: uniq -c prefixes each distinct line with its count.

3.q: What does this do? cat FILENAME | grep -v "#date,food,price,rating" | head -n 3 | cut -d, -f 2
o: Shows the first 3 lines in full
Shows only the first 3 foods, without dates, prices or ratings
3.e: Drop the header, keep 3 lines, then keep column 2.

3.q: What does this print? cat FILENAME | grep -v "#date,food,price,rating" | cut -d, -f 3 | sort -n | tail -n 1
3.e: Numeric sort puts the largest value last.

3.q: Which command correctly lists the foods that cost exactly 5, in alphabetical order?
3.e: Match the surrounding commas so that 15 and 50 are not matched.

4.q: Which path is absolute?
4.e: Absolute paths start at the root with /.

4.q: With the current directory /home/jones, what does ../smith/reports resolve to?
4.e: .. goes from /home/jones to /home; then smith/reports follows.

4.q: What does chmod u=rw,go= file do?
o: Everyone can read and write it
Only the owner can execute it
Only the owner can read and write it
4.e: The owner gets read and write; group and world get nothing.

4.q: Which command removes only an empty directory?
4.e: rmdir fails if the directory is not empty.

4.q: You can ls a folder ABC but cd ABC says "Permission denied". What is missing?
4.e: Directory x means you may enter it.

4.q: Why can two files share a name without a conflict?
o: They sit in different directories, so their full paths differ
4.e: The full path makes a file unique.

4.q: Does renaming report.txt to report.pdf convert the file?
o: No. Only the name changes; the contents stay the same
4.e: The extension is only a hint to the OS.

4.q: After mkdir one .two three, ls shows only one and three. Why?
o: .two is hidden, so ls needs -a to show it
4.e: Names starting with a dot are hidden.

4.q: Why must files in Linux be explicitly given executable permission?
o: So users don't accidentally run a malicious downloaded file
Execute permission only applies to directories
It makes the file load faster

4.q: You run ./this-is-running.sh and get "Permission denied". What is the likely fix?
A teammate can ls the shared file report.docx but gets "Permission denied" when opening it. What is missing?
o: Read permission for the group (or world, if they are not in the group)
4.e: Listing a name needs directory access; opening the file needs read permission.

4.q: Files you put in a folder vanish after every reboot. Using only course content, what is a possible cause?
o: The folder is stored in RAM, which is volatile
The folder is stored on the SSD
4.e: Storage survives a reboot; RAM does not.

5.q: What does an IP address identify?
5.e: IP identifies the computer; the port identifies the process on it.

5.q: The default ports for SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are, in that order ...
nmap reports a port as "filtered". What does that mean?
o: The server is running and listening
The host answered that nothing is listening
A firewall hides the true state, so nmap can't tell
5.e: The probe is blocked, so the state is unknown.

5.q: What does DNS do?
5.e: DNS is the phone book for names.

5.q: Why can packets of one message arrive out of order?
o: Routers delete the number from each packet
5.e: Independent routing means arrival order can differ.

5.q: What defines a LAN?
o: A network over a whole country
A network in a small geographic area such as a building
A network that is only wireless
A network connected through the Internet backbone
5.e: LAN = small area; WAN = large distances.

5.q: What is the purpose of a router in a LAN?
o: To act as a gateway between the LAN and the WAN

5.q: A router receives a packet. What does it know about the packet's journey?
o: The whole route from source to destination
Every route for all packets at once
It needs a human to choose
The best next step toward the destination
5.e: Each router only picks the next hop.

5.q: In the hostname lab1.network.school.edu, what is the top-level domain (TLD)?
5.e: The TLD is the final label.

5.q: ping ex.com complains about a failure in "name resolution". What is the most likely cause?
o: The domain ex.com does not exist
The web server on ex.com is stopped
5.e: Name resolution is the DNS lookup step.

5.q: Why does 127.0.0.1 still work when your device is in airplane mode?
o: It uses mobile data in the background
It is a loopback address that routes traffic within your own device
It connects to a nearby router
Airplane mode does not block anything

5.q: What might happen if two processes tried to use the same port number?
o: They would clash, causing errors or failed connections

5.q: Which analogy best describes packet switching?
o: Sending a long letter as separate envelopes by different routes, then reassembling it
Sending one big parcel along a single fixed route
Writing a letter and never mailing it
Phoning one person on a dedicated line
5.e: Messages are split, routed independently and reassembled.

5.q: nmap shows port 80 as open on a host. What does that indicate?
o: A server process is listening on port 80
5.e: Open means an application is listening.

6.q: Which statement correctly relates the Internet and the Web?
o: The Internet runs on top of the Web
The Web is a system built on top of the Internet
6.e: Infrastructure first, then the Web on top.

6.q: A web page references 5 images. How many HTTP requests does loading it need?
6.e: One for the HTML plus five for the images.

6.q: In https://www.example.com:443/path/page.html?k=v#top, which part is the host?
6.e: The host names the server to contact.

6.q: What does python -m http.server serve by default?
6.e: The current directory becomes the web root, on port 8000.

6.q: A page references extra images. How does the browser fetch them?
o: They are embedded in the HTML file
The client sends a separate HTTP request for each object after getting the base HTML
The browser caches them in advance
6.e: One request for the HTML, then one per object.

6.q: An HTTP server is started. From which folder does it serve files, and why does it matter?
o: The Downloads folder; it doesn't matter
The home folder; it speeds up loading
The web root folder; the wrong folder could expose private files
The root /; it hides hidden files
6.e: Only the web root is served, so choose it carefully.

6.q: What is source HTML?
o: The rendered output of the page
The raw HTML text received by the browser
The IP address of the host
6.e: Source is code; rendered is the displayed page.

6.q: Why is HTTPS preferred over HTTP?
o: It encrypts the data between client and server
6.e: Encryption gives privacy and security.

6.q: In an HTML document, what is the <head> section for?
o: Information about the document, such as its title
The visible content of the page
6.e: <head> holds metadata; <body> holds the content.

6.q:
Computer W (IP 1.2.3.4) will host a website on port 8888, and computer X will access it. The steps are:
Step 1: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is closed.
Step 2: On W, start the web server on port 8888.
Step 3: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 4: On X, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 5: On X, visit http://1.2.3.4:8888 and check that the page appears.
Which step ensures that no other process is already using port 8888?
6.e: A closed port before starting means nobody else is listening on it.

6.q:
Computer W (IP 1.2.3.4) will host a website on port 8888, and computer X will access it. The steps are:
Step 1: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is closed.
Step 2: On W, start the web server on port 8888.
Step 3: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 4: On X, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 5: On X, visit http://1.2.3.4:8888 and check that the page appears.
Which step confirms the web server is running correctly from within W itself? If it fails, the web server is the likely culprit.
6.e: It tests the server locally, before the network is involved.

6.q:
Computer W (IP 1.2.3.4) will host a website on port 8888, and computer X will access it. The steps are:
Step 1: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is closed.
Step 2: On W, start the web server on port 8888.
Step 3: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 4: On X, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 5: On X, visit http://1.2.3.4:8888 and check that the page appears.
Step 3 passes but this step fails, which suggests a firewall on W or between X and W is blocking access. Which step is it?
6.e: Step 4 is the first test from an external computer.

6.q:
Computer W (IP 1.2.3.4) will host a website on port 8888, and computer X will access it. The steps are:
Step 1: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is closed.
Step 2: On W, start the web server on port 8888.
Step 3: On W, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 4: On X, use nmap to check that W's port 8888 is open.
Step 5: On X, visit http://1.2.3.4:8888 and check that the page appears.
Which step confirms that an actual web browser can access the website?
6.e: The goal is for users to reach the site with a browser.

o: Leases private IP addresses to devices that join
Translates private IPs to public IPs

7.q: What does NAT let many devices do?
7.e: NAT maps many private addresses to one public address.

7.q: What does an Optical Network Terminal (ONT) do?
o: Converts optical signals from the ISP into electrical signals for the home network
7.e: The ONT ends the fibre line.

7.q: Why can't every device have its own public IPv4 address?
o: Public addresses are too long to type
There are more devices than public addresses available

7.q: Two routers in separate home networks give two devices the same private IP. What happens?
o: Nothing bad, because the networks are separate
7.e: Private addresses only need to be unique inside one LAN.

7.q: Why is NAT less critical for IPv6?
o: IPv6 has a vastly larger address space
7.e: There is little reason to share addresses.

7.q: Which analogy best contrasts public and private IP addresses?
o: Public IPs are like country names (globally unique); private IPs are like street names (can repeat)
Public IPs are like street names; private IPs are like country names
Both are like phone numbers on the same exchange
7.e: Street names repeat across countries; country names do not.

8.q: Which cloud model is open to any subscriber?
8.e: Public clouds such as AWS are multi-tenant.

8.q: What does terminating an EC2 instance do?
o: Pauses billing but keeps the disk
Wipes the machine and stops billing
8.e: Terminate is like turning the computer off for good.

8.q: In ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@IP, what does -i supply?
8.e: -i names the private key used to authenticate.

8.q: Why does ssh refuse a key.pem with loose permissions?
o: The private key must not be readable by others
8.e: If others can read it, it is not private.

8.q: What is the purpose of launching an EC2 instance?
o: To get a virtual server in the cloud that runs applications
8.e: EC2 is a rented virtual machine.

8.q: What happens if the private key file is deleted?
o: You are locked out and cannot connect over SSH

8.q: In an inbound security rule, what does the source 0.0.0.0/0 mean?
o: Any IPv4 address on the Internet

8.q: In the EC2 launch screen, what is an "OS Image" such as Amazon Linux?
o: A pre-configured template with an operating system, used to create an instance
8.e: You don't have to install the OS from scratch.

8.q: Port 80 is not allowed in the EC2 security group but the HTTP server is running. What does a browser see?
o: A long wait, then "This site can't be reached"

9.q: A DoS flood crashes a web server. Which CIA pillar is attacked?
9.e: Authorised users can no longer reach the service.

9.q: Which key does Alice use to encrypt a message to Bob in public-key cryptography?
9.e: Only Bob's private key can then decrypt it.

o: It checks incoming traffic and filters unwanted traffic
9.e: It enforces an access control policy.

9.q: What does a certificate authority do?
o: Verifies a public key by issuing a digital certificate

9.q: What is the main weakness of symmetric encryption?
o: Both sides must share the same key, which can be intercepted

9.q: What is the difference between false acceptance and false rejection in biometrics?
o: Acceptance admits an unauthorised user; rejection blocks a legitimate user

9.q: Why is cryptography needed even when users have strong passwords?
o: Strong passwords can't be typed over a network
It protects the content itself, so it can't be read even if a password is compromised
Passwords are always stored in plaintext
Cryptography replaces the need for authentication
9.e: Passwords protect access; cryptography protects the data.

9.q: Which sequence correctly describes Alice sending Bob an encrypted message with public-key cryptography?
o: Bob encrypts with his private key; Alice decrypts with her public key
Alice gets Bob's public key, encrypts the message with it, sends it, and Bob decrypts with his private key
Alice and Bob share one secret key beforehand and both use it
Alice encrypts with her private key and Bob decrypts with it

10.q: An IoT startup runs an assisted-living platform on an Amazon EC2 instance, protected by a security group. Which ports does the security group open to the whole Internet?
10.e: Web ports are public; SSH is admin-only.

10.q: Why does the developer first host the server on 127.0.0.1:8000?
o: Loopback is faster than the Internet
To test rendering without exposing unfinished code

10.q: What shares the home's single public IP among the sensors and laptops?
10.e: NAT maps private addresses to the one public address.

cards.d: The physical parts of a computer that you can touch, such as the processor, memory, storage and ports.
Programs and data that run on the hardware, including the operating system and applications.
Fetches, decodes and executes instructions and processes data; the only part that actually computes.
Cycles per second. 2.8 GHz is 2.8 billion cycles per second.
An independent processor inside a multi-core CPU. More cores help parallel work but cost more power.
Very fast volatile memory on or near the CPU that holds frequently used data. Checked before RAM.
Volatile memory that holds the OS, programs and data in use. Its contents are lost when power is off.
Non-volatile secondary memory for the OS, applications and files. Slower than RAM.
An SSD has no moving parts, so it is faster and more durable. An HDD has a spinning disk, so it is slower, cheaper and more fragile.
Memory that loses its contents when power is removed, such as RAM and cache.
Kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, tera 10¹², peta 10¹⁵. The course uses powers of ten.
A processor for graphics that relieves the CPU. It is also used for machine learning and parallel matrix work.
Pixels wide × high. 1920 × 1080 is 1,920 pixels across and 1,080 down. The screen size in inches is the diagonal.
A computer dedicated to a narrow range of functions inside a larger system, such as a microwave, car or watch.
Both instructions (software) and data are stored in the same memory unit.
Software written to address specific user needs, such as a browser, office suite or game.
Software that manages the computer at a fundamental level and runs applications. Windows, Linux and macOS are examples.
The core of system software. It manages resources, provides a user interface and lets applications use resources. All of this is "sharing nicely".
Programs take turns on the CPU so that all make progress.
Each process gets an isolated space in RAM, which is reclaimed when it ends.
On power-up, firmware loads the OS (kernel) from non-volatile storage into memory and hands control to it.
A GUI is clicked and tapped. A CLI is typed. The CLI is strongest for batch work, automation and remote administration.
Commands are lowercase; options come before arguments; the order of options does not matter. Tab completes, the arrows recall history.
An executable file with instructions, stored in non-volatile storage.
A program in execution. It lives in RAM and terminates at power-off.
The foreground process is the one you interact with. Background processes run without direct interaction.
Lists processes you own. Written without a dash.
Ctrl-c terminates the foreground process. Ctrl-z suspends it.
bg resumes the suspended process in the background. fg resumes it in the foreground.
List files; long format with permissions and size; include hidden files that start with a dot.
Show the whole file, the first 10 lines, or the last 10 lines. -n N changes the count.
Extracts fields. -d sets the delimiter and -f picks fields, e.g. cut -d"," -f2.
Prints lines matching a pattern. -i ignores case; -v prints lines that do not match.
Sorts lines. -r reverses; -n sorts numerically; the default is alphabetical.
Removes adjacent duplicate lines. -c counts, -d shows duplicates, -u shows unique lines. Sort first.
Counts lines in the input.
Sends the output of one command to the input of the next.
* matches zero or more characters; ? matches exactly one.
> creates or overwrites a file; >> appends to it.
Prints from line 2 onward, which skips a header row.
cut the column, sort, uniq -c, sort -n -r, head -n N.
A named collection of related data used to organise secondary memory.
A named group of files, also called a folder. A directory tree lets the same filename appear in different directories.
Both are stored as bits. A text file holds characters you can read in a text editor; a binary file needs special software to interpret its bits.
The part after the dot that suggests the file type. Renaming does not change the content or convert the file.
A path from the root directory. It always starts with / and identifies one file uniquely.
A path from the current working directory. It never starts with /.
. is the current directory and .. is the parent directory.
A colon-separated list of directories searched, in order, for executables. The first match is run.
cp copies and the source stays. mv moves or renames and the source goes away.
rmdir removes only an empty directory. rm -r removes a directory and everything inside it.
A name that starts with a dot. ls hides it; ls -a shows it.
u = owner, g = group, o = everyone else, a = all three.

cards.t: r, w, x on a file
cards.d: Read the contents, modify the contents, run it as a program.

selfq:
Think first, then open the answer. These mix recall, explain-why, calculation and apply questions.

Q1 (recall). List the four things every packet must carry and say which identifies the computer and which the process.

Answer

Destination IP, destination port, source IP, source port. IPs identify the computer; ports identify the process (§5.4).

Q2 (explain why). Why must sort precede uniq in a pipeline?

Answer

uniq only removes adjacent duplicates; sort makes equal lines adjacent first (§3.2).

Q3 (calculation). A laptop lists 20 GB RAM. How many bytes is that, and about how many 4-byte emoji could fit ignoring overhead?

Answer

20×10⁹ = 20,000,000,000 bytes; /4 = 5×10⁹ emoji (five billion) (§1.3).

Q4 (apply). Write one pipeline that prints how many distinct ratings appear in yum.csv, then state the answer.

Answer

tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f4 | sort | uniq | wc -l → ratings A, B, C ⇒ 3 (from the dataset in §3.3).

Q5 (apply). Using yum.csv, which command lists the three most expensive prices?

Answer

tail -n +2 yum.csv | cut -d',' -f3 | sort -n -r | head -n 3 → 20, 15, 12 (computed from the dataset).

Q6 (compare). Compare chmod u=rw,go= f with chmod u=rw,go=r f.

Answer

Both give the owner read/write. The first removes all access for group and world (private, e.g. SSH key); the second lets them read only.

Q7 (apply). Your CWD is /home/jones/projects. What absolute path does ../../smith/reports resolve to?

Answer

.. → /home/jones; ../.. → /home; then smith/reports ⇒ /home/smith/reports.

Q8 (apply). You run ./backup.sh and get Permission denied. What do you do and why was it designed this way?

Answer

chmod u+x backup.sh. Linux requires explicit execute permission so a downloaded file can't run accidentally (§4.8).

Q9 (trace). Starting in an empty directory, what does ls show after mkdir a .b c, and what shows .b?

Answer

ls shows a c; ls -a shows .b too (and ./..).

Q10 (explain why). Why does ls ../kiwi work from grape but cd kiwi fails there?

Answer

../kiwi goes up to charlie then kiwi; plain kiwi is a relative path under grape, which has no kiwi.

Q11 (apply). A process was suspended by accident. Give the exact keystrokes/commands to end it.

Answer

fg then Ctrl-c (§2.6).

Q12 (compare). Compare program, process, foreground process, background process.

Answer

Program = file in storage; process = running program in RAM; foreground = receiving your input; background = running without it.

Q13 (apply). A web page references 7 images and 1 stylesheet. How many HTTP requests does the browser make?

Answer

1 (HTML) + 7 + 1 = 9.

Q14 (apply). You start python -m http.server 8080 in ~/Documents. A friend on your LAN opens http://:8080. What risk exists?

Answer

Everything in ~/Documents is browsable by anyone on the LAN — wrong web root (§6.5).

Q15 (apply). http://localhost:8000/fruits/../animals/cat/page1.html maps to which file?

Answer

public_html/animals/cat/page1.html (the fruits/.. cancels out).

Q16 (apply). Which of these are private IPs: 10.9.9.9, 172.20.1.1, 172.40.1.1, 192.169.0.1, 192.168.255.1?

Answer

10.9.9.9 ✔, 172.20.1.1 ✔ (within 172.16–31), 172.40.1.1 ✘ public, 192.169.0.1 ✘ public, 192.168.255.1 ✔.

Q17 (explain why). Why can your neighbour and you both use 192.168.0.10?

Answer

Private addresses aren't routable on the Internet and are only meaningful within one LAN; separate LANs never conflict (street-name analogy) (§7.2).

Q18 (trace). Trace a laptop (192.168.0.12) visiting a site through a router with public IP 203.0.113.45.

Answer

Laptop → router; router NAT replaces source with 203.0.113.45 (+ new port) and records the mapping; site replies to the public IP; router looks up the mapping and forwards to 192.168.0.12 (§7.4).

Q19 (diagnose). ping example.com fails with "name resolution" but ping 1.1.1.1 works. What's wrong?

Answer

DNS resolution is failing, but basic connectivity is fine.

Q20 (diagnose). nmap host -p 80 says filtered while the web server is running. Most likely cause?

Answer

A firewall/security group is dropping port-80 probes (e.g. no inbound rule for 80).

Q21 (compare). Compare nmap closed and filtered.

Answer

Closed: host replies, nothing listening. Filtered: no usable reply because a firewall blocks; the true state is unknown.

Q22 (explain why). Why does 127.0.0.1 still work in airplane mode?

Answer

Traffic loops back inside the device's own network stack; no external network is used.

Q23 (compare). Compare symmetric and public-key encryption.

Answer

Symmetric: one shared key; the key must be exchanged securely (if intercepted everything is compromised). Public-key: public key encrypts, private key decrypts; the private key never travels.

Q24 (calculation). Encrypt NETWORK with the Caesar shift-3 cipher.

Answer

N→Q, E→H, T→W, W→Z, O→R, R→U, K→N ⇒ QHWZRUN.

Q25 (calculation). Decrypt VHFXULWB (shift 3).

Answer

V→S, H→E, F→C, X→U, U→R, L→I, W→T, B→Y ⇒ SECURITY.

Q26 (classify). Map each incident to a CIA pillar: (a) leaked patient file; (b) altered account balance; (c) site down under request flood.

Answer

(a) Confidentiality; (b) Integrity; (c) Availability.

Q27 (apply). Your EC2 web server runs on port 80 but the browser times out. List checks in order.

Answer

(1) ping/connectivity; (2) dig if using a name; (3) nmap IP -p 80: filtered ⇒ add an inbound Security Group rule for 80 from 0.0.0.0/0; closed ⇒ start the server; open ⇒ check content/web root.

Q28 (apply). ssh refuses your key file. What command fixes it and why?

Answer

chmod u=rw,go= is114-keypair.pem — SSH rejects keys readable by others.

Q29 (evaluate). A team proposes SMS codes as their 2FA. Evaluate.

Answer

It meets "two factors", but SMS is unencrypted in transit, vulnerable to SIM-swapping and phishing; CISA recommends against it — prefer an authenticator app/hardware token.

Q30 (case). In the IoT case study, name the tier and technology that stops the public Internet from reaching SSH.

Answer

Tier 4: the AWS Security Group inbound rule restricting port 22 to administrator IPs (a firewall/access control policy) (§J).

Q31 (case). Why do developers test on 127.0.0.1:8000 before deploying to EC2?

Answer

It keeps unfinished code and flaws off the public Internet and needs no external network (§J).

Q32 (compare). Compare on-premise vs public cloud vs hybrid.

Answer

On-premise: you own/maintain hardware. Public: rent from a provider, pay-as-you-go, any subscriber. Hybrid: combine private/on-premise (e.g. sensitive data) with public (e.g. web front end).
